claims.claim_text: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids; the only trick is to cook it no more than medium, since well-done or burnt fat forms heterocyclic amines. He even recommends raw steak tartare.
claims.verbatim:
Red meat is an unequaled source of animal protein and essential 
lipids - the secret is to not eat meat cooked well done or eat the fat 
burnt as they become heterocyclic amines. Medium rare and medium are the safe way to eat beef. Steak Tartar is a half pound of raw, 
freshly ground sirloin, served with chopped onions, pepper corns 
and topped with a raw egg - it doesn’t get any better than this!

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites a 930-woman study where eating beef and pork very well done raised breast-cancer risk 462% versus medium-rare; his point is that it is not the fat but the cooking that harms you, because burnt animal fat becomes heterocyclic amines, powerful carcinogens.
claims.verbatim:
On November 18, 1998, Dr. Wei Zheng of the University of South 
Carolina reported that in a study of 930 women, those who ate their 
beef and pork cooked very well done increased their risk of breast 
cancer by 462 percent over those women who ate their meat cooked 
medium rare - it is not the amount of fat in the diet that counts, but 
rather, how you cook the fat that counts. Burnt animal fat is converted to heterocyclic amines which are extremely powerful carcinogens.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's 'Feedlot Syndrome' analogy: ranchers fatten beef cattle on a steady stream of carbohydrate feed paired with optimal nutrients that drive the animal to eat with endless, fervent hunger, growing a 40-lb calf to 900-1,100 lb in a year. He argues humans are fattened by the same carb-heavy diet — but, unlike the optimally-supplemented cattle, humans eat it while mineral-deficient, which is what leaves them with a ravenous appetite.
claims.verbatim:
Raising prime beef successfully, requires a steady stream of carbohydrate, protein and fat calories in the proper ratios specifically 
designed for fattening. 
The intense weight gain, high carbohydrate diet must be accompanied by optimal mixes of nutrients designed to encourage weight 
gain and drive the animal to eat with an endless and fervent hunger. 
Feed, based on corn or other carbohydrates, is made available in 
a steady stream. Beef cattle will grow from a forty pound calf to 900 
- 1,100 pounds in about a year under optimal feedlot conditions.

claims.claim_text: Not on its own, in Wallach's view. He points to the Old Order Amish, who eat pork, beef, goat and mutton 3 times a day plus heavy whole milk, butter and cheese — by his account consuming more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than anyone in North America — and yet post an obesity rate of just 4% and a type-II diabetes rate of just 6%, only about a tenth and a half, respectively, of their 'modern' neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their meat-heavy diet, and not even to their hard farm labor (the horses do most of the work), but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every single morning.

Wallach cites a Scientific American longevity summary: the patients who followed doctors' advice to the letter didn't reach 100, while the 'rebellious' ones who ate salt, eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did.
claims.verbatim:
the individuals who followed their doctors advice to the 
letter, didn’t make it to 100 years of age, while people who ate salt, 
eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did.

claims.claim_text: Pellagra turned out to be a dietary deficiency disease — a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin) — and eggs were part of the fix. Wallach recounts how a U.S. Public Health Service researcher noticed that in orphanages and mental asylums the residents came down with pellagra while the staff, who ate a wider variety of food, stayed well. When eggs and milk were simply added to the sufferers' diets, the pellagra disappeared. Wallach lays out the competing theories of the era — the main one blamed the limited corn diet, while some held that pellagra was an insect-borne disease like malaria or yellow fever, and sufferers were isolated in federal centers as though they were contagious like tuberculosis — and this is his illustration that nutrient-dense foods like eggs can reverse a 'disease' that was really malnutrition.
claims.verbatim:
When eggs and milk were 
added to the diet of the affected individuals, pellagra disappeared.

claims.claim_text: Yes — and it was more than a footnote. Wallach was a co-petitioner on the FDA petition (Docket No. 03Q-0401, filed 6/23/2003) that won the qualified health claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk, which the FDA allowed on 9/8/2004. It matters because it was one front in Wallach's larger legal war against the FDA — waged with First Amendment attorney Jonathan Emord — to force the agency to let supplement makers state health benefits that were actually proven. The same campaign carried his solo selenium-and-cancer claim (approved 4/28/2003); as he tells it, after losing every battle before the 1994 DSHEA Act, his side won every one that followed. So the official omega-3 heart-health language products can now use is partly his doing.
claims.verbatim:
Petition for Amended Health Claim. Omega-3 Fatty Acids and

160 
Coronary Heart Disease (Co-Petitioner); Docket No. 03Q-0401; 
filed on 6/23/2003. qualified claim allowed by FDA on 9/8/2004.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's maintenance dose for the liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals: one ounce per 100 pounds of body weight per day, ideally split. A 100-pound person takes one ounce a day (or half an ounce — one tablespoon — twice daily); a 200-pound person, two ounces; a 300-pound person, three, and so on. He specifies the supplement should carry at least 77 minerals at a concentration of 19,000 mg per quart and cover all 90 essential nutrients. For anyone needing to lose 25 pounds or more, the level can be raised to one and one-quarter ounces per 100 pounds.
claims.verbatim:
These liquid minerals should be taken at the rate of one ounce 
per hundred pounds of body weight as a maintenance dose. For example, a 100 pound person would take one ounce per day in a split 
dose or one half ounce (one tablespoon) twice per day. A 200 pound 
person would take two ounces per day; a 300 pound person would 
take three ounces per day and so on. 
For those individuals needing to lose twenty five pounds or more 
the supplement level can be increased to one and one quarter ounces 
(1 1/4 oz) per 100 pounds of body weight

claims.claim_text: Wallach's tactic for sugar cravings and the munchies while quitting sugar: take one ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 pounds of body weight — even up to ten times a day at first. He reads cravings and pica as a sure sign of mineral deficiency, so flooding the body with absorbable minerals is meant to switch the urge off.
claims.verbatim:
If during the process of giving up sugar you get the “munchies” 
or feel the need to go on the classic “chocoholic” binge, take one 
ounce of plant derived colloidal minerals per 100 pounds of body 
weight - even if it’s ten times per day at the start (remember - cravings 
or pica are the sure sign of mineral deficiencies!!).

claims.claim_text: A practical use for the liquid complex: distilled water is mineral-free and over time pulls minerals out of the body, so Wallach suggests re-mineralizing it — add one ounce of liquid colloidal minerals (at 19,000 mg of minerals per quart) to each gallon of distilled or double-filtered water.
claims.verbatim:
A good compromise is to use distilled or double filtered water 
that has been “enriched” with liquid colloidal minerals at the rate of 
one ounce of the liquid colloidal minerals (19,000 mg of minerals 
per quart) per gallon of distilled or double filtered water.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's own outcome evidence for the complex, from a 2004 pilot study he co-authored among the Nez Perce of Idaho (Wallach, MacCoy, Henry, and Schrauzer). On a plant-derived colloidal mineral program — framed as replacing the wood ashes the tribe historically got their minerals from — almost all participants lost weight, significantly lowered their blood pressure, and cut fasting blood sugar by thirty to fifty percent, with everyone able to significantly reduce or come off their medication.
claims.verbatim:
A 2004 pilot supplement study (Wallach, J.D., MacCoy, B., Henry, 
L. and Schrauzer, G.N.) with the Nez Perce Indians of Idaho, has 
shown that almost all participants lost weight, significantly reduced 
blood pressure and reduced fasting blood sugars by thirty to fifty 
percent. All were able to significantly reduce or wean off of their 
medication.

claims.claim_text: ORAC stands for Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity, a lab score for how strongly a food, drink or supplement neutralises free radicals. The test scores one specific attacker, the peroxyl radical, chosen because it is among the most common reactive oxygen species in the human body. Worth noting that Wallach's books print the name two ways - Absorbance in Immortality, Absorption in Hell's Kitchen.
claims.verbatim:
A good way to measure the antioxidant activity of foods including juices is by means of the ORAC point system. ORAC stands for 
Oxygen Radical Absorption Capacity, a measure of the scavenging

claims.claim_text: Wallach's practical trick is to replace salad dressing with a high-ORAC juice - noni or mangosteen - instead of oil. It sits inside his See Food Diet, where oils and dressings are a main target. For eating out he gives the Salad Fork Trick: dip the fork a quarter inch into the dressing and shake off the excess, which lets you taste it while giving up about ninety-five percent of the calories.
claims.verbatim:
At home you will want to use a high ORAC value juice (noni, 
mangosteen) or juice blend for a salad dressing. When dining out 
you will want to use “Dr. Wallach’s Salad Fork Trick.” 
Dr. Wallach’s Salad Fork Trick is simply performed by dipping a 
salad fork 1/4 inch into the dish of salad dressing and shaking off the 
excess. This simple procedure will allow you to taste the salad dressing, yet give up ninety five percent of the calories

claims.claim_text: Losing weight itself creates the damage antioxidants defend against. Wallach says the byproducts of burning fat can turn into free radicals that inflame the intima, the lining of the arteries, which then drives arteriosclerosis, cardiovascular disease, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. His instruction is not a single daily pill but flooding yourself with multiple antioxidants at every meal, framed as an insurance policy against the free radicals you will eat without knowing it.
claims.verbatim:
To reduce the risk of the complications 
of weight loss, people need to flood themselves with antioxidants in order to protect themselves.

claims.claim_text: Wallach classes common supplement forms such as zinc gluconate as 'metallic minerals,' which in his framework are poorly absorbed. He states that metallic minerals — sold as gluconates, lactates, sulphates, carbonates and oxides — are only eight to twelve percent biologically available in younger people, and that after age thirty-five to forty their availability plummets to three to five percent. This is the basis for his preference for plant-derived colloidal minerals, which he considers the most efficient form of trace-mineral supplement.
claims.verbatim:
Typically, metallic minerals are found in tablets and powders as 
gluconate (calcium gluconate, zinc gluconate, etc.), lactate, sulphates, 
carbonates and oxides (iron oxide, etc.). 
Metallic minerals, despite wild claims to the contrary are only 
eight to twelve percent biologically available to younger animals and 
humans; after attaining the age of thirty five to forty years, the availability of metallic minerals plummets to three to five percent.

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to a National Cancer Institute five-year study in Henan Province, China, that tested nutrients against a placebo in about 29,000 people aged forty to sixty-nine. He reports that zinc — along with vitamin C, retinol, riboflavin, molybdenum and niacin — had no statistically significant protective effect on cancer deaths after five years. By contrast, the group taking a combination of beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium saw dramatic results: 13% fewer deaths from all cancers, a 21% reduction in stomach-cancer deaths, and a 9% drop in deaths from all causes. In Wallach's account, zinc was not among the standout cancer-protective nutrients in that trial.
claims.verbatim:
The investigators reported that, “vitamin C, retinol, zinc, riboflavin, molybdenum and niacin had no statistically significant (protective) effect on cancer deaths after five years.” 
The group that took the combination of beta carotene, vitamin E 
and selenium for five years had dramatically positive results: 13 percent fewer deaths from all cancers, 21 percent reduction in deaths 
from stomach cancer and a 9 percent decrease in deaths from all 
causes.

claims.claim_text: Among nuts, Wallach singles out cashews as a good magnesium source: a handful supplies about 20 percent of the USDA recommended daily allowance of magnesium, along with 30 percent of copper and 10 percent of iron. An ounce — roughly 18 roasted nuts — carries 160 calories and 13 grams of fat.
claims.verbatim:
Cashews: a handful contains 20 percent of the USDA recommended daily allowance of magnesium, 30 percent of copper, and 
10 percent of iron. One ounce (18 roasted nuts) contains 160 calories and 13 grams of fat.

claims.claim_text: Among nuts, Wallach singles out English walnuts as nutritionally special: they are a good source of iron, phosphorus, zinc, potassium, and vitamin E, and — uniquely — the only nut with significant levels of omega-3 fatty acids, the anti-inflammatory fats usually associated with fish. An ounce (about 14 halves) carries 190 calories and 18 grams of fat. He raises them within a broader point that nuts, far from being junk food, are tied to lower rates of heart disease.
claims.verbatim: Walnuts: English walnuts are a good source of iron, phosphorus, zinc, potassium, and vitamin E; they are the only nut with significant levels of omega-3 fatty acids. One ounce (14 halves) contains 190 calories and 18 grams of fat.

claims.claim_text: Wallach considers the Metabolic Syndrome a product of multiple nutrient deficiencies rather than genetics. In his deficiency table he lists omega-3 essential fatty acid deficiency as producing elevated total cholesterol, elevated LDL, obesity, peripheral neuropathies, thrombotic disease, and atherosclerosis.
claims.verbatim:
Omega -3 essential fatty acids elevated total cholesterol, elevated 
LDL, obesity, peripheral neuropathies, thrombotic disease, atherosclerosis

claims.claim_text: Wallach points to a November 2003 Tufts University analysis of fatty-acid blood levels from 1,137 Framingham Heart Study patients, followed for about ten years for new dementia including Alzheimer's. He reports the finding that those with diets rich in omega-3 fatty acids had a significant 48 percent reduction in the risk for the onset of dementia.
claims.verbatim:
On November 18, 2003, researchers at Tufts University reviewed 
the fatty acid levels of blood collected from 1,137 patients on the 
Framingham Heart Study, their diets were assessed and those free of 
dementia were followed for a mean of ten years. During the study 
they were assessed for the onset of new dementia including Alzheimers 
disease. Those with, “diets rich in Omega-3 fatty acids had a significant 48 percent reduction in the risk for the onset of dementia.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that Dr. Linus Pauling, a double Nobel Prize winner, championed large doses of vitamin C in his book Vitamin C and the Common Cold, both for fighting colds and for preventing cancer and heart disease. Pauling recommended that individuals take 10 to 12 grams of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) each day - far above ordinary intakes.
claims.verbatim:
Pauling recommends that individuals take 10 - 12 
grams of ascorbic acid or vitamin C each day.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in 1928 the biochemist Albert Szent-Gyorgyi found that capsicum, or cayenne peppers, are rich in vitamin C. This makes peppers one of the concentrated dietary sources of the vitamin.
claims.verbatim:
In 1928, Albert Szent-Gyorgyi, an American biochemist found 
that capsicum or cayenne peppers are rich in vitamin C.

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites a January 2004 Johns Hopkins University study of 4,740 men and women over age 65 which found that those taking vitamin C and vitamin E together had a 78 percent reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease. He groups this with other antioxidant and omega-3 findings, concluding that antioxidant intake can substantially lower the onset of Alzheimer's.
claims.verbatim:
On January 20, 2004, researchers from the Johns Hopkins University School of Public Health, released the results of a study on 
4,740 men and women over the age of sixty five that showed, those 
taking vitamin C and vitamin E had a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s 
disease by 78 percent.

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites a 1993 National Cancer Institute study of 29,000 people in China's Henan Province, which found that vitamin C - along with retinol, zinc, riboflavin, molybdenum and niacin - had no statistically significant protective effect on cancer deaths after five years. By contrast, the group taking beta carotene, vitamin E and selenium had markedly better results, with fewer cancer deaths. In this trial vitamin C on its own did not lower cancer mortality.
claims.verbatim: The investigators reported that, “vitamin C, retinol, zinc, riboflavin, molybdenum and niacin had no statistically significant (protective) effect on cancer deaths after five years.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in 1933 Tadeus Reichstein became the first person to produce a vitamin synthetically in the laboratory, and that his artificial form of vitamin C was identical to the natural one. In other words, lab-made ascorbic acid is chemically the same molecule as the vitamin C found in food.
claims.verbatim:
In 1933, Tadeus Reichstein has become the first to produce a 
vitamin synthetically in the laboratory, and his “artificial form of vitamin C is identical to the natural one.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in 1922 it was established that the original vitamin A actually consisted of two separate factors. The original growth factor retained the name vitamin A, while the anti-rachitic (anti-rickets) factor was designated vitamin D. Fortification of milk with vitamin D soon followed in the United States.
claims.verbatim:
In 1922, it was established that the original vitamin A consisted 
of two separate factors. The original growth factor retained the name 
vitamin A, while the anti-rachitic factor was designated vitamin D.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's framework, deficiencies of two or more essential minerals produce significant pica, cravings, and binge eating. He states that iron and phosphorus deficiencies occurring at the same time will result in an almost psychotic binge eating and soft-drink consumption rampage that ends in morbid obesity. The craving, in his view, is the mineral-starved body driving the person to eat — not simple gluttony.
claims.verbatim:
The deficiency of two or more essential minerals will produce a significant level of pica, cravings and binge eating. Iron 
and phosphorus deficiencies occurring at the same time will result in an almost psychotic binge eating and soft drink consumption rampage that results in morbid obesity.

claims.claim_text: In Hell's Kitchen, Wallach frames calcium as a weight-control mineral: consuming 1,200 mg of calcium each day, even if you do nothing else, will reduce your risk of being overweight by sixty-five percent. If you are already overweight, cutting 500 calories a day (about one burger) while taking the 1,200 mg of calcium will double your rate of weight loss—he says, even without the need for exercise.
claims.verbatim:
We know that if you do nothing else, consuming 1,200 mg of ) 
calcium each day will reduce your risk of being overweight by sixty 
five percent! If you are overweight, give up 500 calories each day 
(one burger), and consume the 1,200 mg of calcium per day and you 
will double your rate of weight loss - even without the need for exercise!

claims.claim_text: In 1755 the Spanish physician Gaspar Casal (1680-1759) published an account of pellagra — a vitamin B3 deficiency — then considered 'a new disease' in Spain. He described it by the 'Three D's': dermatitis (a horrible dry, scabby crust crossed with cracks), diarrhea, and dementia, plus premature death, and noted the disease flared up each spring.
claims.verbatim:
In 1755, Gaspar Casal (1680-1759), published an account of 
pellagra (a vitamin B3 deficiency), then “a new disease” in Spain. 
Pellagra is characterized by the “Three D’s” including dermatitis (“a 
horrible crust, dry, scabby...crossed with cracks”), diarrhea, dementia and premature death - this disease flared up each Spring.

claims.claim_text: In his discussion of nuts, Wallach points to pistachios as a source of vitamin B6: a handful supplies twenty-five percent of the USDA recommended daily value. One ounce (50 dry-roasted nuts) contains 160 calories and 13 grams of fat.
claims.verbatim:
Pistachios: a handful of pistachios gives twenty five percent of 
the USDA recommended daily value for vitamin B6.

claims.claim_text: Discussing alcohol and breast cancer, Wallach notes that one large study put the lifetime risk of breast cancer at 8.8 percent in nondrinkers and 10.1 percent in women who consume two drinks per day. He adds that research also shows folic acid supplementation can reduce the risk of breast cancer for nondrinkers and drinkers alike. In his framing, folic acid is protective regardless of alcohol intake.
claims.verbatim:
One large study indicates that the lifetime risk of breast cancer is 
8.8 percent in nondrinkers and 10.1 percent in those women who 
consume two drinks per day - research also shows that folic acid 
supplementation can reduce the risk of breast cancer for nondrinkers and drinkers alike.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in 1925 the pathologist George Hoyt Whipple bled dogs to produce anemia, then fed them varying diets to see which best rebuilt red blood cells. Dogs that ate liver — which is rich in iron, copper, selenium, vitamin B12, vitamins A, C, and D, folic acid, and essential fatty acids — formed red blood cells more quickly than the others. The passage highlights liver as a dense natural source of folic acid and the other blood-building nutrients.
claims.verbatim:
In 1925, Dr. George Hoyt Whipple, an American pathologist took 
large amounts of blood from dogs to produce anemia. Whipple fed 
the dogs varying diets to learn how different diets affect the production of red blood cells. He recorded that dogs that ate liver, which is 
rich in iron (and copper, selenium, vitamin B12, vitamin A, vitamin 
C, vitamin D, folic acid and essential fatty acids), formed red blood 
cells more quickly than those that did not.

claims.claim_text: Wallach charges that the FDA's 1963 restrictions on folic acid remained in place for thirty-one years. He notes that by 1998, following the institution of folic acid supplementation, the spina bifida rate had dropped by twenty percent. Only in 1996 did the FDA, in his words 'being dragged, kicking and screaming to the end,' finally order folic acid fortification of flour.
claims.verbatim:
The 1963 restrictions on folic acid remained in place for thirty 
one years - by 1998, and the institution of folic acid supplementation, the spina bifida rate had dropped by twenty percent. 
In 1996, the FDA (being dragged, kicking and screaming to the 
end), finally orders folic acid fortification of flour.

claims.claim_text: Wallach holds that salt is the raw material the body uses to manufacture stomach acid, and that stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) is what digests food, ensures mineral absorption, activates the digestive enzyme pepsin, and activates the 'intrinsic factor.' That intrinsic factor is exactly what is needed to absorb vitamin B12. By this logic, restricting salt undercuts stomach acid and can therefore drive a vitamin B12 deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Salt is the raw material needed to manufacture stomach acid. 
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid that is necessary to digest food, 
ensure absorption of minerals, activate pepsin (protein digestive enzyme produced by the stomach) and activate the “intrinsic factor”

HELLS KITCHEN 257 
necessary to absorb vitamin B12.

claims.claim_text: In 1849 Thomas Addison described a fatal anemia, later named pernicious anemia, marked by a low count of abnormally enlarged red blood cells. Vitamin B12 was eventually identified as the missing nutrient, but the disease had a second twist: the stomach must produce two things, stomach acid and an acid-dependent 'intrinsic factor,' or B12 cannot be absorbed. Wallach notes that B12 injections can cure the disease by bypassing the stomach entirely, and that stomach-acid substitutes like betaine HCl can be used to reactivate intrinsic factor and restore absorption.
claims.verbatim:
In 1849, Thomas Addison reported the existence of a hitherto 
unknown fatal anemia, that was eventually called pernicious anemia 
- it was characterized by a low red blood cell count, but the cells that 
were observed were enlarged red blood cells. Vitamin B12 was eventually identified as the missing essential nutrient, however, there was 
another feature unique to pernicious anemia - the stomach had to 
produce two important substances: 1) stomach acid and 2) an acid 
dependent cofactor known as “intrinsic factor” - without either or 
both vitamin B12 could not be absorbed.

claims.claim_text: In tracing how early humans got their minerals, Wallach describes animal organs — the heart, livers, kidneys, and brains — as rich in stored minerals such as selenium, zinc, and copper (and vitamins including B12, A, C, and D). He presents organ meats as a dependable dietary source of copper.
claims.verbatim:
The 
animals organs, including the heart, livers, kidneys and brains were 
rich in stored minerals such as selenium, zinc and copper

claims.claim_text: Wallach notes that a handful of cashews contains about 30 percent of the USDA recommended daily allowance of copper, plus 20 percent of magnesium and 10 percent of iron. This makes cashews one of the concrete everyday foods he cites as a copper source.
claims.verbatim:
Cashews: a handful contains 20 percent of the USDA recommended daily allowance of magnesium, 30 percent of copper, and 
10 percent of iron.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that a decade before Einstein's death his team had eliminated ruptured aneurysms in turkeys simply by increasing the copper in their feed pellets. Despite the best doctors money could buy, he says Einstein died of a simple copper deficiency, and that Einstein had shown warning signs of it for decades in the form of grey hair and deep skin wrinkles.
claims.verbatim:
ten years earlier we had eliminated ruptured aneurysms 
in turkey’s (a cause of devastating losses) by simply increasing the 
copper levels in their food pellets. 
We are sure that Einstein had the very best doctors that money 
could buy and that medical science could provide - yet Einstein died 
of a simple copper deficiency - a deficiency that he had warnings of 
(grey hair and deep skin wrinkles) for decades before he died.

claims.claim_text: In Wallach's framework chromium is an essential trace element the body must have for normal glucose metabolism, and its function is tied directly to insulin. It is the working core of GTF, the glucose tolerance factor (a complex of chromium III, dinicotinic acid, and glutathione), and only the trivalent form is biologically active. The whole body holds only about 1.5 mg, yet Wallach considers chromium so central to blood-sugar control that he names its deficiency, together with vanadium, a primary cause of diabetes and hypoglycemia. He cites the USDA's Richard Anderson that ninety percent of Americans are deficient in it.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium is required for circulating glucose tolerance factor to 
function properly. Chromium is an essential trace element necessary 
for the normal glucose metabolism, It’s function is directly related to 
the function of insulin.

claims.claim_text: Wallach explains that only the trivalent state of chromium is biologically active, working by forming complexes with organic compounds. Chromium's role is not limited to glucose metabolism. Animal studies show it also stimulates amino acid transport and protein synthesis.
claims.verbatim:
Only the trivalent state of chromium is biologically active and it 
works by forming complexes with organic compounds. Insulin-chromium relationships are not restricted to glucose metabolism. Animal 
studies have shown that chromium stimulates amino acid transport 
and protein synthesis.

claims.claim_text: Wallach characterizes chromium deficiency by glucose intolerance — hypoglycemia, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia, and diabetes. It also produces poor growth, peripheral neuropathies, and a negative nitrogen balance, meaning loss of muscle mass or sarcopenia. A decreased respiratory quotient is another sign.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency of chromium is characterized by glucose intolerance 
(hypoglycemia, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinemia and diabetes), 
poor growth, peripheral neuropathies, negative nitrogen balance (loss 
of muscle mass - sarcopenia) and a decreased respiratory quotient.

claims.claim_text: Wallach says chromium and vanadium deficiencies show up as a thirst for liquids like soft drinks, juices, and alcohol, with plain water the last choice, plus an obsessive hunger for carbohydrates of all kinds. The 'munchies' and cravings for alcohol and candy, especially chocolate, are in his view sure signs of a chromium and vanadium deficiency. He cites Reagan's craving for jelly beans as an example.
claims.verbatim:
Chromium and vanadium deficiencies are manifested by thirst 
for liquids (soft drinks, juices, alcohol, etc.), with water being the 
last choice and an obsessive hunger for carbohydrates of all types. 
The “munchies,” cravings for alcohol and candy cravings (Regan’s 
cravings for jelly beans), especially chocolate, are sure signs of a chromium and vanadium deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites K. N. Jeejeebhoy, who by 1977 reported that chromium could eliminate the need for medical insulin in human patients. His intravenous use of chromium in human diabetics eliminated peripheral neuropathies and removed the need for insulin treatments to stabilize blood sugar. Wallach uses this as evidence that chromium addresses the root of the disease.
claims.verbatim:
By 1977, K. N. Jeejeebhoy reported that chromium could eliminate the need for medical insulin in human patients. His intravenous 
use of chromium in human diabetics eliminated peripheral neuropathies and well as eliminated the need for insulin treatments to stabilize blood sugar.

claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that potassium-deficient laboratory rats become hyper-alert and hyperactive and start licking everything within reach — their metal cage, lab equipment, each other, and even urine puddles. Even under a severe potassium deficiency, he notes, the rats still show a strong craving for sodium chloride (common salt). He uses these animal observations to show how a mineral shortfall can drive compulsive licking and craving behavior.
claims.verbatim:
Potassium deficient rats are hyper alert, hyper active and tend to 
lick everything including their metal cage, lab equipment, each other 
and urine puddles (beer and urine have a similar taste). It is also 
interesting to note that even with a severe potassium deficiency laboratory rats have a strong craving for sodium chloride (salt).

claims.claim_text: Wallach says a natural potassium deficiency is highly unlikely, because grains, fruits and vegetables all tend to be rich in potassium (the K in NPK fertilizer). Where it does appear, he points to two causes: taking diuretics, and eating a diet where the only 'vegetable' is French fries and ketchup. In his view, genuine deficiency usually comes from drugs or a produce-free diet rather than from ordinary eating.
claims.verbatim:
A natural potassium deficiency is highly unlikely in nature, as all 
grains, fruits and vegetables tend to be rich in potassium (NPK fertilizer) - a potassium deficiency can be found in individuals given diuretics and individuals whose only vegetable intake is French fries 
and ketchup.

claims.claim_text: Wallach recounts that in April 1925 the Morton Salt Company placed an ad in the Woman's Home Companion to market iodized salt as a new table salt that prevents goiter. The pitch promised that "Nature's iodine restored" would prevent goiter, then described as threatening almost every child, with no change in taste. Adding iodine to salt became a public-health fix once physicians identified insufficient iodine in the thyroid as the cause of goiter.
claims.verbatim:
“Now - a new table salt that prevents goiter. Save children! Nature's 
iodine restored - yet tastes no different.
